boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Brice's Cross Roads record (June 10, 1864) in Forrest's Defense of Mississippi [June-August 1864]: the engagement at the cross-roads and the rout to Tishomingo Creek on the 10th. The June 7-9 skirmishes, the pursuit and the fight at Ripley on the 11th and the retreat to Collierville are context. Expedition-wide marches, captures, destruction and loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field gives the Union column as a three-brigade infantry division and a cavalry division, about 8,500 (side bound 8,500); NPS gives Forrest's cavalry corps as about 2,000, and the live field reads 10500 (US 8500; CS 2000). Sturgis gives his command in round numbers as about 8,000, listing brigades of 1,500, 1,800, 2,000, 1,000 and 1,200, and says his officers estimated the enemy at 15,000 to 20,000. Forrest gives his available force as 3,500 and the enemy's, from prisoners and captured documents, as 10,252; his June address speaks of not over 3,000 against 10,000. He says his orders had been to move into Middle Tennessee with 2,000 of his own men and 1,000 of Roddey's.
claims.rationale: Round figures of each commander for his own side and estimates of the other, at different scopes; the frozen and live Confederate figures have no inspected basis. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: Sturgis says the artillery and wagons were mired at Ripley after continuous rain, that the dense woods at the cross-roads made it hard to use his guns, and that on the retreat the road became jammed and wagons and guns sank into the mud. Forrest says the undergrowth was so dense that Bell's brigade advanced within thirty yards before assaulting, and that abandoned vehicles blocked the road before Tishomingo Creek.
claims.rationale: Ground and weather described by the two commanders; no map verification.

claims.value: Sturgis says his train of some 250 wagons carried rations for eighteen days, that his animals were exhausted and starved by the time he reached Ripley, and that about 200 wagons and 14 guns were lost on the retreat with cartridge-boxes nearly empty. Forrest reports 250 wagons and ambulances, 18 guns, 5,000 small-arms and 500,000 rounds taken, and says his own horses were jaded; his June address gives 17 guns, 250 wagons and 3,000 stand of arms.
claims.rationale: Losses and captures from the two commanders; the counts of wagons, guns and arms differ and none is adopted. No supply return.

claims.value: Sturgis says that at Ripley all of Washburn's information and his own led to the conclusion that there was no considerable force in his front, though his information was meager, and that the enemy learned his movements from the population while he could learn theirs only by fighting. He says Grierson first reported some 600 of the enemy (read 'GOO' in OCR). Forrest says he learned on the night of the 9th that the enemy was encamped on the Guntown road, and hoped to reach the cross-roads first.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Major General Nathan Bedford Forrest and Brigadier General Samuel D. Sturgis; the live page styles Sturgis Major General. Sturgis says he decided at Ripley, against his forebodings, to go on, directed Grierson and the infantry at the cross-roads, and that Winslow's cavalry led the flight to Stubbs'. Forrest says he led Bell's brigade around to the Guntown and Ripley road, ordered Buford to press the center and right and bring up the artillery, and credits Barteau's regiment in the Union rear.
claims.rationale: Command roles from the two commanders; the listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit, and the live rank is not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory. Sturgis wrote on June 11 that his command had lost most everything after a very hard fight and in his report that his army yielded to overwhelming numbers; Forrest says the enemy's retreat or rout began at the cross-roads and calls it one of the most complete victories of the war.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty field reads 3,105 (US 2,610; CS 495); the live field reads 3103 (US 2610; CS 493). Sturgis's table is garbled in OCR but ends 'Total killed, wounded, and missing, 2,240'; he says his principal officers supposed the enemy's killed and wounded fully as great as his own. Forrest gives his loss in killed and wounded, from the chief surgeon, as 493, the enemy's killed and wounded as not less than 2,000 and prisoners as not less than 2,000; the provost-marshal's report counts 1,618 captured.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Forrest's 493 matches the live Confederate figure; the frozen 495 and both Union totals of 2,610 have no inspected basis, and Sturgis's 2,240 covers the expedition, not only June 10.

open_questions: McMillen's, Grierson's, Waring's, Winslow's and the other Union reports (Nos. 3-19), the Board of Investigation (No. 20), S. D. Lee's No. 21 report, the Confederate casualty return (No. 23; garbled), Forrest's quartermaster and ordnance inclosures (garbled), Jordan and Pryor's Chapter XVIII and maps remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family (the NPS battle page plus the frozen Arnold rows). Nathan B. Forrest's reports of July 1 and August 4, 1864, the provost-marshal's report forwarded with the first, his June 1864 address and his August 21 Memphis dispatch as relayed by Maury (Official Records Series I, Volume XXXIX, Part 1, Nos. 22, 45 and 15) are one family of interested Confederate accounts. The Official Records volume is a shared container, not an additional witness; report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge. Here the second family is Samuel D. Sturgis's June 11 dispatch and June 24 report (No. 2), written after he asked for an investigation of his defeat.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
